properties.Name: Hippodrome Theater
properties.WhyShort: After being closed for many years, 2011 renovations led to the theater reopening.
properties.WhyLong: Having originally closed in 1945 due to a fire, the Hippodrome underwent renovations and reopened in 2011. The Hippodrome serves a similar purpose to what it did when it originally opened, it is a place where people go for concerts, parties, and private events. The theater serves as a way to educate young people about the history of Jackson Ward and the role African Americans played in building the United States.

properties.Name: I-95
properties.WhyShort: Built in the middle of Jackson Ward cutting it in half and disrupting many homes and businesses.
properties.WhyLong: In the 1950s, I-95 bisected Second Street and Jackson Ward as a whole. A block wide path was carved through the ward displacing an estimated 1,000 households and destroying hundreds of historic homes, buildings, and neighborhood structures. With construction ending in 1958, disruptions to the neighborhood were far from over. Today, about 150,000 cars per day drive along this portion of I-95 creating constant noise pollution. Along with this, the Northern section of Jackson Ward continues to be cut off from Historic Jackson Ward with less access to businesses and services.

properties.Name: Maggie Walker Historic Site
properties.WhyShort: A national park devoted to perserving the legacy of Maggie Walker.
properties.WhyLong: Opening in 1975, the Maggie L. Walker National Historic Site is the country’s first national park devoted to an African American woman. Maggie Walker was the first American woman to establish and head a bank. Along with this, Walker was the founder and president of the Richmond Council of Colored Women and worked to improve health care for African Americans. The historic site is preserved and furnished exactly how Maggie Walker left it.

properties.Name: Mama J's Kitchen & Mural
properties.WhyShort: Serving the community since 2009, Mama J's Kitchen has become a Jackson Ward staple.
properties.WhyLong: Velma Johnson founded Mama J’s Kitchen in 2009. She was taught how to cook from her mom but her dad was also a culinary expert himself as he was a head cook for the Life of Virginia Insurance Company. She was a deputy sheriff for 17 years of her life but catering was calling her name and thus she resigned from her job to do full time catering. Mama J’s Kitchen was founded and opened in 2009 in a building on North 1st street in historic Jackson Ward. It’s been a staple to the Jackson Ward community ever since as Mama J’s continues to treat her customers like family. On the corner of 1st and Clay street resides a mural of Black culinary icons of Richmond Virginia. The mural includes Velma “Mama J" Johnson, John Dabney, Edna Lewis, Neverett Eggleston, and the building of Miller’s hotel.

properties.Name: Jackson Center
properties.WhyShort: Parts of historic East Clay Street were cleared to build this center.
properties.WhyLong: Today, the Jackson Center is home to Virginia Commonwealth University's MOTIVATE clinic and adult outpatient psychiatry along with the Historic Jackson Ward Association. For this building’s construction, many historic buildings off East Clay Street had to be destroyed.

properties.Name: The Speakeasy Grill
properties.WhyShort: Is in the restored Taylor Mansion and serves as a place of food and entertainment for the community.
properties.WhyLong: The Speakeasy Grill today is housed in W.L. Taylor’s Old Mansion. The restaurant highlights Southern cuisine and it is a reference to the Prohibition era when alcohol was banned. Thus, at this time mansions would be used as speakies to freely drink alcohol. The actual speakeasy is towards the back of the mansion which has dark lighting and high ceilings and all sorts of entertainment can be going on at any time from Jazz to spoken word.

properties.Name: Mocha Temple No. 7 Shrine Club & Mural
properties.WhyShort: Fraternal organization that hosts social activities and raise money for children's charities.
properties.WhyLong: The Mocha Temple No. 7 Shrine Club houses the fraternal organization, the Mocha Shriners, who primarily raise money for children charities and serve communities. They also hold many social events and activities like parades. On the side of the Mocha Temple No 7. Shrine Club is a mural of the first all-Black professional fire crew in the city of Richmond. On July 1st, 1950 10 black men were appointed to Engine Company #9. These men were Charles L. Belle, William E. Brown, Douglas P. Evans, Harvey S. Hicks II, Warren W. Kersey, Bernard C. Lewis, Farrar Lucas, Arthur L. Page, Arthur C. St. John and Linwood M. Wooldridge. It was very important to this community to have this representation because imagine your livelihood, your home, on fire and a firefighter turning away because of the color of your skin. They gave the community pride.
